NEW YORK (CNN) — A prosecutor said Saturday that a man accused of bringing a bag filled with wires and batteries into New York’s LaGuardia Airport, prompting alarm and a major evacuation, has been ordered to receive a psychiatric assessment.

Officials were treating LaGuardia Airport’s Central Terminal as a crime scene. Authorities said 32-year-old Scott McGann appeared in court after walking into the terminal Saturday morning with an object later determined to be a fake bomb. The terminal was shut down for several hours before reopening.

Queens District Attorney Richard A. Brown said McGann faces charges of first-degree placement of a false bomb or hazardous substance, placing a false bomb or hazardous substance in a transportation facility, and making terrorist threats.

Although McGann was in court Saturday, Brown said his arraignment was delayed. He is being held without bail.

“The defendant is clearly a very troubled young man,” Brown said. “As a result, the Court has directed that he be examined to determine whether he has the capacity to understand the proceedings against him and assist in his defense.”

Earlier, authorities said McGann would not talk to his attorney or to anyone else. He is due back in court Thursday.

According to investigators, McGann entered a terminal checkpoint around 4:50 a.m. with a backpack and declined to respond to security questions. Authorities said the checkpoint officer was told that a suspicious item was fastened to the underside of McGann’s backpack. McGann then allegedly took hold of what looked like a triggering device with a red button attached to the backpack.

Investigators said McGann pushed the button multiple times before a Port Authority officer seized both the trigger and the package from him.

Brown said the package was found to be a device made up of batteries, cylinders and electronic parts that could have been used in bomb-making. However, the bomb squad determined it contained no explosives.

A law enforcement official familiar with the investigation said McGann had a ticket for a United Airlines flight to Chicago, along with seats on two additional connecting flights, with Oakland, California, as his final destination.

The source told CNN that McGann had been arrested three previous times in the New York area. The latest case involved June charges of evidence tampering and resisting arrest. He had also been arrested twice in 2008, the source said.

Port Authority spokesman John Kelly said McGann “was just acting crazy.” Kelly said the officers who arrested him described him as “extremely disheveled and dirty,” in a “near catatonic state,” and “staring off into space.” McGann had been homeless for at least one year.

Authorities cleared the terminal after 5:20 a.m. By midmorning, passengers were allowed to return to all sections except Concourse C, Kelly said. Federal Aviation Administration spokeswoman Holly Baker said the concourse reopened shortly before 11 a.m.

Flights at the airport had been temporarily halted, with no takeoffs or landings allowed, but Baker said operations resumed shortly after 9 a.m.

The Central Terminal is one of LaGuardia’s four terminals. The airport is located in Queens, roughly eight miles from Manhattan.

The incident interfered with travel for many passengers. An American Airlines spokesperson said the airline canceled 16 flights. American Eagle, Continental Airlines and Southwest also reported delays.

CNN i-Reporter Jose Ojeda, 24, said he was on a plane bound for Chicago, Illinois, sitting on the tarmac when the evacuation was ordered. Ojeda, who is from the Bronx, New York, said his flight had been scheduled to depart at 6:10 a.m.

“We were all ready to go,” he said. “They didn’t make any announcement other than, ‘You need to evacuate.’”

“At first I thought it was standard procedure,” Ojeda said, “but then once we got out of the plane, they kept pushing us back and back, out of the terminal, out of the actual airport.”

CNN’s Chuck Johnston, Aspen Steib, Ross Levitt, Laurie Segall and Susan Candiotti contributed to the report.
